thread: Euclid's geometric treatment of vision and light propagation is the ancestor of every optical system. The solar gravity lens mission exploits geometric optics at cosmic scale — bending light around the Sun to form an image of distant worlds.

Ibn al-Haytham's Book of Optics established that light enters the eye — it doesn't emanate from it. His analysis of refraction and lens behavior is the intellectual foundation for every telescope, including FLUTE's liquid-lens approach to space optics.

Archimedes' principle of buoyancy — that a body in fluid is buoyed up by a force equal to the weight of fluid displaced — is directly used to design the Titan submarine's ballast and depth control in liquid methane.

Kepler proved planetary orbits are ellipses governed by mathematical laws. StarNAV extends this: if orbital mechanics are predictable, then the apparent positions of stars from a moving spacecraft encode the spacecraft's own trajectory. Navigation by stellar aberration is Kepler's laws running in reverse.

Galileo pointed a telescope at the Moon and saw craters. Four centuries later, we want to build a telescope inside one of those craters — using the Moon's far side as the quietest radio observatory in the solar system.

Ptolemy built the most detailed star catalogue of the ancient world and modeled planetary positions for 1400 years. HOEE continues the quest to map the heavens — but now we're looking for Earth-like planets orbiting those stars.

Democritus proposed that all matter is composed of indivisible particles moving in void. 2400 years later, lattice confinement fusion exploits the atomic structure of metal lattices to confine deuterium nuclei closely enough to fuse — the atom as both prison and fuel.

Kepler's third law — the relationship between orbital period and distance — defines the energy budget for every deep-space mission. The PuFF engine exists because chemical rockets can't beat that budget fast enough: reaching Pluto in 4 years requires breaking out of Kepler's gentle curves.

Copernicus moved the Sun to the center. Five centuries later, we want to use that central Sun as a gravitational lens — its position at the heart of the solar system isn't just a fact of astronomy, it's an optical resource.

Hero of Alexandria described the aeolipile — the first known steam engine — in 62 CE. SPARROW is a steam-powered hopping robot designed for icy moons: it melts ice for water, flash-boils it, and uses the steam to leap across Europa's surface. Hero's principle, applied to another world.

Al-Khwarizmi gave us algebra — the language of equations. Every gravitational model, from Newton's inverse square law to general relativity's field equations, is written in the mathematical language he helped create. GODEX uses that language to hunt for dark energy's fingerprint.

Eratosthenes measured Earth's circumference using shadow angles and geometry — remote sensing 2300 years before satellites. Cryospheric Rydberg Radar is remote sensing at its most extreme: using quantum-sensitive atoms to peer through kilometers of ice on Europa from orbit.

Vesalius built anatomy on empirical observation rather than ancient authority. Astropharmacy takes the same principle to space: rather than trusting that pre-packaged drugs will survive years of radiation and temperature cycling, synthesize medicine on demand from first principles.

William Gilbert proved Earth is a giant magnet. Earth's magnetic field shields us from cosmic radiation. This NIAC concept asks: can we generate a spacecraft-scale magnetic field to create the same shield? Gilbert identified the natural protection; this concept tries to replicate it artificially.

Napier invented logarithms to simplify the astronomical calculations of his era. The metamaterial solar sail's design requires optimizing electromagnetic response across wavelengths — computations that would have been impossible without the mathematical tools Napier's invention eventually enabled.
